problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Create a “Story-Thread” wall: volunteers string a 20 m clothesline across the room at eye level. Each participant writes a personal sentence on a numbered paper strip, hangs it, then ties the strip’s loose end to the previous strip. Over 90 minutes the line becomes a single interwoven story. Participants later receive a printed map of the thread showing everyone’s number so they can reconnect by phone or social media. Cost: 8 euros for string, 12 euros for markers and paper, 5 euros for printing; total under 30 euros. Six volunteers manage stations and refreshments; no equipment beyond the room is needed.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A two-hour "Recipe Relay" begins with each of six volunteers bringing one inexpensive, locally available ingredient (total ≤300 €). Participants pair randomly, exchange brief personal stories while preparing a shared dish, then swap partners and ingredients mid-session. After three rotations, all six dishes are tasted together. A wall-sized sheet of paper invites each person to add their contact details and one takeaway, forming an instant community cookbook. The empty room becomes the venue; volunteers handle setup and cleanup. No special tools beyond basic kitchen utensils are needed, and the event can start next weekend.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants lay objects on the table and attach one colored tag—"Fix," "Parts," or "Story"—in five minutes. "Fix" items receive a 15-minute paired repair slot using shared tools; "Parts" items are disassembled for spares; "Story" items are documented with a one-sentence label and displayed. Any item still tagged "Fix" after its slot moves automatically to "Parts." Success is measured by counting objects diverted from landfill (tags logged) and anonymous exit slips rating participation 1-5; 70 % of participants scoring ≥4 and ≥60 % objects diverted counts as success.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Volunteers hang 60 simple paper envelopes in the room, each labeled with a unique number. Every resident receives a blank postcard and an envelope number at signup. Over two weeks they write and post one card to that number. On the final evening, envelopes are opened simultaneously; each person reads their received card aloud to the group. The activity costs under 50 euros for envelopes, string, postcards and tea, needs only a table and chairs, and creates an immediate, shared story that continues through follow-up postcard exchanges.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Each participant writes one numbered step of the skill on a separate card. Cards are shuffled and laid face-down. In round-robin, a learner draws the next card, reads it aloud, then physically demonstrates that step with the group watching; any gaps are filled by collective recall. After all steps are enacted, the group re-orders the cards into the correct sequence on a table and checks the final arrangement together. Success is observable when the ordered sequence matches the intended order and every learner can perform the full skill without referring to cards.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Learners pair up and each pair receives one unique, 12-step practical skill broken into 12 index-card steps. In hour one, pairs teach their step to the room in a rapid 5-minute carousel, then return and receive the next card. In hour two, they reassemble the sequence on a wall, test the skill, and adjust cards until the sequence works without gaps or errors. Success is observable when the group can execute the full skill correctly on the first try at the end of hour two.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants label each object with a 'story tag' (memory or emotion). Objects are placed on the table and sorted into three zones: repairable, transformable, or memorial. A rotating 'skill circle' of three volunteers demonstrates one safe technique per zone (glue, sanding, decoupage) for five minutes. Any participant may attempt the technique on any object. A red 'pause token' on the table lets anyone stop work if confidence drops. Success is assessed by counting objects that leave with a participant (repaired, transformed, or kept as art) versus those recycled, targeting at least 60 % retention.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A 'Story Exchange Circle' pairs six volunteers with residents in rotating duos. Each person receives two €5 gift cards and a blank postcard. Over three weekly 90-minute sessions, partners swap five-minute personal stories, then write one anonymous takeaway on the postcard to be pinned on a community map. The final gathering uses the remaining €270 budget for simple snacks and printed name-tags, creating a permanent, growing exhibit of shared narratives that newcomers can continue adding to indefinitely.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A three-round peer-teach relay. Divide twelve learners into four trios. In each 20-minute round, two members of a trio teach the third the skill using only the available stationery; after 15 minutes the roles rotate so each person both teaches and learns. At the hour mark trios swap and repeat, so every learner is taught by three different peers. Success is observable: at the end of the second meeting each trio must demonstrate the full skill together without notes, and the librarian records whether the demonstration is completed correctly within five minutes.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Each participant brings one household item that requires a precise two-step adjustment (e.g., replacing a bike inner tube or setting a sewing-machine tension). In hour one, pairs exchange items and silently observe each other’s micro-movements for five minutes, then verbally label every motion using only stationery-drawn arrows and numbered labels on a shared sheet. In hour two, pairs swap roles and repeat, now annotating corrections on the same sheet. Success is observable when every pair’s final sheet shows a correct, numbered sequence that another pair can follow without clarification, verified by a live demonstration using the annotated item.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Volunteers host a "Memory Map Walk" where pairs of strangers receive a shared town map and a list of 12 everyday spots. They spend 90 minutes visiting three chosen spots together, asking each other one prompted question at each place and marking a shared memory on the map. After the walk, pairs return to the room, add their marks to a single large map on the wall, and briefly tell the group one story. The process repeats with new pairings over four weekly sessions. Total cost: 40 euros for markers, tape and tea; the rest buys snacks. No tools or experts needed beyond printed maps and the volunteers’ time.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A Story-Stitch Circle: volunteers collect six second-hand fabrics (under 5 € each) and cut them into 30 cm squares. Over two weeks, residents are invited in pairs to embroider or paint a single shared symbol representing a local landmark or memory on one square. Pairs meet for 30 minutes, swap a short personal story, then sign the square. Completed squares are sewn together into a wall-hanging displayed in the town hall lobby. The low-cost, no-skill format encourages repeated visits and creates a visible, lasting record of new acquaintances.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants bring one broken object and one spare part or fastener they can spare. They draw lots to pair with a different object. Using only table, hand tools and their parts, they attempt a reversible modification that turns the item into a new household function rather than restoring the original. A colored tag marks any join that must stay accessible for later disassembly. After two hours, each maker photographs the result, writes a one-sentence use note, and places it on a shared display table. Success is tallied by counting how many tagged objects are claimed for home use within one week and by logging how many original parts remain reusable. Unclaimed items go to local scrap collection.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants first sort the 20 objects into “Try,” “Parts,” and “Keep” bins, guided by a 5-minute demo of safe disassembly. Two volunteers log each item on a shared sheet. A rotating “buddy pair” rule pairs any participant with another before touching tools, providing a safeguard. Each repaired or repurposed item earns a sticker on a visible wall chart; success is measured by the ratio of stickers to original objects after two hours. Unfixed items are disassembled for spare parts or art, ensuring zero landfill waste while keeping involvement optional and pressure-free.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A "Story-Seed Exchange" pairs residents randomly at a 2-hour drop-in twice weekly. Each person receives a 2-euro blank postcard and a prompt (e.g., "A place that felt like home"). After writing, participants swap cards, read privately, then add one line in response. Cards are pinned to a wall map of the town, forming a growing collage. The six volunteers rotate as hosts, supplying markers, string, and refreshments from the budget. Newcomers receive a colored pin to mark their card, visibly showing expanding ties. After four sessions the map is photographed and printed as free postcards for participants, creating a portable reminder of new bonds.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Residents bring one meaningful object and a short story to a "Memory Market." Six volunteers label six tables "family," "hobby," "challenge," etc. Each participant places their object on a matching table and briefly tells their story to the group already there. After five minutes, a bell rings; everyone moves to the next table of their choice. After six rounds, participants receive a printed card listing the names and contact details of people whose stories they heard, creating instant follow-up pairs. Total cost under 50 euros for cards, markers and simple snacks; the rest of the budget funds a shared follow-up picnic two weeks later.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Twelve adults are paired for a 30-minute ‘teach-back’ session: one person writes a concise step-by-step guide to the target skill on a shared sheet; the partner then silently performs each step while the writer corrects in real time. Roles swap for the second half-hour. The next week, each participant must demonstrate the skill to the group in under two minutes using only the revised sheet; success is measured by whether the observers can replicate the skill on first attempt without verbal help.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Learners form a chain: each writes one step of the skill on a card and passes it clockwise; next adds the following step, folds the prior card out of sight. After twelve cards, the chain reverses; each reads aloud only their step and demonstrates it on scrap paper. The group reconstructs the full sequence by matching written steps to demonstrated actions. Success is observed when every participant can recite and perform the entire chain without cards, verified by a silent walk-through clocked under five minutes.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: The group divides into three teams of four. In hour one, each team silently writes a 200-word mini-manual on the skill using only blank cards and markers, then swaps manuals. In hour two, each team attempts the skill guided only by the received manual while the originating team silently observes and records three observable success checkpoints on a shared wall chart. At the end, teams compare achieved checkpoints; the method succeeds when at least two checkpoints per team are visibly marked as met, confirming that the exchanged manuals enabled observable skill transfer without external instruction.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A rotating ‘Story-Chain’ evening: volunteers collect 30 household objects (books, tools, toys) from neighbors and label each with a memory prompt. On night one they arrange the objects in a circle; every participant draws one, shares the prompted story for two minutes, then hands it to the next person, who adds a new detail. After four rounds the objects are swapped for new ones brought by newcomers. A shared notebook records the chain of additions. Total cost: 20 euros for snacks and marker pens. Two volunteers host, two collect objects, two document stories. The cycle repeats weekly for six weeks, each time mixing fresh participants and stories, steadily knitting the town into a living archive of shared memory.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants label each item with a quick color sticker—red for ‘repair together’, yellow for ‘parts donor’, green for ‘keep as-is art’. A ten-minute walk-around lets everyone vote by placing tokens. The three red items with most tokens are tackled first at the single table; the others are immediately disassembled or decorated. A rotating ‘helper card’ ensures a confident participant always partners with a less-confident one. Leftover parts go into a clearly marked community-parts bin. Success is measured by counting how many red items leave functional and how many people stayed to the end; a whiteboard tally gives instant visible feedback.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A 90-minute "Story-Exchange Potluck" begins in the empty room. Each participant brings one simple dish and a small photo or object tied to a personal memory. Volunteers arrange a circle of chairs and a folding table. After a 5-minute welcome, pairs swap stories for 10 minutes, then rotate. Each person ends with a postcard of the person they spoke with, noting one shared interest. A volunteer pins the postcards to a corkboard that stays on the wall for two weeks, turning the room into an open gallery. Cost: 30 euros for postcards, pins, and a simple banner; the rest covers snacks. No special skills or gear required.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Volunteers host a six-session "Story-Swap Potluck" in the empty room. Each 90-minute evening, pairs of residents share a dish and a 5-minute personal story prompted by rotating cards (childhood hero, first job, hidden talent). After eating, pairs exchange contact details on index-card "passports" kept in a communal binder. The binder travels to the next session so new pairs can read prior entries and continue conversations. Six volunteers rotate as hosts; each brings one shared dish and one prompt card set. Total cost: 6×€50 food stipends = €300. Starts in ten days; no special gear needed.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: The 'Recipe Relay' is a single-session, budget-limited event. Residents form six pairs and receive one of six ingredient cards (total cost 35 €). Each pair prepares one course of a shared meal in the room using provided kitchen basics. A 30-minute rotation ensures every participant collaborates with five others. After cooking, the group eats together and each person writes a short recipe card for their favorite new contact. Cards are exchanged, forming immediate keepsakes. Cleanup is shared, ending within three hours. Total cost: 65 €. No specialist equipment is needed.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants form pairs around the table. Each pair picks one broken object and spends five minutes listing its material and last intended use. They then attempt a reversible, non-destructive modification using only the supplied hand tools that turns the object into a new, clearly different everyday item. If the attempt risks further damage, the pair must stop and place the object in a marked discard bin. After all pairs finish, the group votes on the three most useful new items; success is measured by counting how many objects leave as new items versus how many enter the discard bin. Any object left untouched counts as neutral and is removed from the site.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Each participant receives one numbered index card describing one sequential step of the skill. In session one, learners form a silent human chain: each demonstrates their step with stationery props while the next person observes and mimics. The chain repeats until every member can perform the entire sequence. For session two, learners randomly reorder the cards and must re-assemble the chain correctly within fifteen minutes, observed by two peers who log errors on a shared tally sheet. Success is observable when the reordered chain completes without tally marks and all twelve participants can individually recreate the skill unassisted.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Pairs receive one sheet each showing a distinct everyday object drawn with eight deliberate errors. Every 10 minutes they swap sheets, mark new errors, and add one rule explaining the previous owner's marks. After four rounds the group pools rules into a single checklist. Each participant then redraws their original object from memory using the checklist; success is counted by fewer errors on the second drawing. The iterative swap forces error-pattern recognition and collective rule refinement, observable via before-and-after counts.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants label each object "fixable," "parts," or "display" and place it on the corresponding table zone. The "parts" zone is disassembled into fasteners, wood, metal, and fabric bins; reusable components are logged on a shared sheet. A visible two-person rule applies to every tool use. Success is measured by the number of items diverted from landfill and the logged count of participants who handled at least one tool or bin. A rotating "helper" badge lets newcomers shadow experienced fixers without pressure.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Learners form four triads. Each triad receives a shuffled deck of twelve index cards, each bearing one step of the target skill written in plain language. In Meeting 1, triads silently sequence their cards, then rotate clockwise every 10 minutes to critique and reorder the other decks. Consensus sequences are taped to the wall. In Meeting 2, triads rehearse the steps aloud in order, then perform a live 60-second demonstration for the other groups. Success is observable: the librarian notes whether all triads finish their demonstrations without consulting notes and whether the demonstrated sequence matches the final wall chart.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A "Swap-and-Share" circle: objects are laid on the table and each participant tags one with a single Post-it noting a non-repair use (art, planter, spare parts). Tools stay central; anyone may demonstrate a 2-minute technique on any item. A red "pause" card on the table lets anyone stop unsafe work instantly. After 45 min, participants vote by placing a token on the item they most want to adopt or repurpose. Success = ≥60 % of objects leave with a new owner or clear reuse plan; tokens are counted publicly and recorded on a shared sheet.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Place the twenty objects on the table and run a two-hour "swap-repair" session. Participants first sort items into three zones: fixable, parts-donor, and keep-as-is. A volunteer with a clipboard records each item’s status. In the fixable zone, two people work together—one reads a one-page laminated guide (created on-site) while the other performs the repair using only the supplied tools. Parts-donor items are disassembled; usable screws, fabric, or motors are bagged and labeled. Keep-as-is objects receive a sticker noting "display only." A safeguard: no repair exceeds fifteen minutes; if stuck, move the item to parts-donor. Success is assessed by counting (a) items that leave functional, (b) bags of salvaged parts, and (c) participants who report increased confidence on a three-question exit card.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Pairs rotate every 10 minutes through four skill stations pre-loaded with step cards; each pair records the next learner’s progress on a shared wall chart with colored dots. After both sessions the chart shows a complete, color-coded path for all twelve, making mastery visible at a glance.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Learners form four trios; each trio invents one step of a three-step skill (e.g., knot-tying). Using paper strips and pencils, they create a 12-page flip-book: every page shows one illustrated step plus a peer-check question. At meeting one, trios draft their pages, swap them for peer edits, and test the entire sequence on themselves. Meeting two, each person demonstrates the full sequence to the other eleven while peers mark their checklist. Success is counted when at least ten of twelve learners receive all checks within the hour.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants form two concentric circles. Outer-circle members receive one blank index card each; inner-circle members receive a single shared sheet of paper and one pen. In 10-minute rounds, outer members silently write one concise step of the target skill on their card and pass it inward. Inner members must integrate every new card into a single, coherent written procedure on their sheet. After four rounds, the circles swap roles. In the second hour the newly-written procedure is read aloud and each member silently performs the next step in turn while the group verifies it matches the sheet. Success is observable when the completed sheet contains an error-free, sequential procedure that all twelve participants can execute without further guidance.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A repair circle: at a single table, participants first sort the 20 objects into 'try,' 'parts,' and 'no-go' piles. 'No-go' items are disassembled for reusable fasteners and materials; the rest move to 'try.' Each volunteer picks one object, receives a 15-minute tool tutorial, then works with a partner. A red flag on the table halts unsafe work instantly. After 90 minutes, objects are photographed and logged as repaired, repurposed, or recycled. Success is tallied by counting items diverted from landfill and number of first-time participants who complete a task.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Neighborhood "SwapBench" session: place the table outdoors, mark three zones—Fix, Parts, Scrap. Participants start with a 10-minute silent browse, then self-select an object and a partner. Each pair has 20 minutes to diagnose, then decide: repair with tools, harvest reusable parts, or responsibly scrap. A visible "Help Flag" (red cloth) on the table lets anyone summon a quick confidence boost from a rotating mentor. Success is tallied by a running tally of objects leaving each zone and post-session show-of-hands rating (1–5) for enjoyment and learning; ≥70 % positive ratings and ≥60 % objects diverted from landfill marks the event worthwhile.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A two-week 'Story-Seed Exchange' begins with volunteers turning the empty room into a free public library of personal artifacts. Each resident donates one small, meaningful object and writes its story on a card. Twice weekly, volunteers host drop-in evenings where newcomers randomly pair objects, then spend 15 minutes interviewing their new partner about the item’s meaning. Pairs exchange contact details and pledge one future shared activity. All supplies cost under 300 euros: index cards, pens, string, and simple snacks. After two weeks, the room becomes a permanent exchange board where stories and objects stay visible, allowing ongoing, self-sustaining connections.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: 'Shared Story Tiles' turns the empty room into a living storybook. Six volunteers collect 20 second-hand picture frames (under 5 euros each) and printed local photos or drawings. Over two evenings, participants pair up, pick one frame, and write a 50-word micro-story about a town memory it evokes. Each pair swaps frames and adds one sentence, then hangs the finished tiles in a temporary gallery. A simple rota lets new visitors continue the chain each week, steadily weaving strangers into a collective narrative anchored by visible, growing artwork.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Form two fixed teams of six. Session 1: each team receives six identical 20-step origami instructions and 50 blank cards. Members silently fold the first model, then write one clear step onto a card. Cards are shuffled and redistributed; each person must reconstruct the sequence from the new cards. Success is measured by how many cards produce the correct next fold. Session 2: the teams swap decks and repeat the reconstruction under a five-minute time cap. Observable metric: both teams must achieve ≥80 % correct sequence matches in the timed round.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A Repair-or-Repurpose Carousel: participants form a circle with the table at center. Each person presents one broken object, names one function it might still serve, then passes it clockwise. The next person may attempt a 90-second fix with the tools or declare it “repurpose-ready.” If no one fixes it after two full rotations, the object is tagged for disassembly or donation. A red “pause card” lets anyone stop unsafe work. Success is measured by tallying fixed items plus parts salvaged for future neighborhood projects; a simple chart on the table tracks both numbers so the group sees the reduction in waste at a glance.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants form three-person teams around one broken object. Each team first tags its object “repairable,” “parts,” or “art.” A 15-minute rotating tool-share cart lets anyone borrow pliers or tape without leaving the table. After 45 minutes, teams display the object with a two-sentence label: either how it now works or why it became an installation. Success is measured by a show-of-hands count of teams that finish a label and by a simple waste tally: objects leaving the table divided by twenty. A posted “pause rule” halts work if any participant feels unsafe or overwhelmed, ensuring inclusive pacing.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants label each object with a single shared rating: "worth fixing," "parts only," or "material." They spend 15 minutes as a group choosing only the three highest-rated items for repair. A "timekeeper" volunteer limits work to 45 minutes per item and halts if the item is still non-functional. Leftover pieces go into labeled bins for future projects or recycling pickup. Success is assessed by counting how many chosen items become usable again and by a quick show-of-hands vote on whether the process felt inclusive and low-pressure.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants create a shared, hand-drawn "skill wall"—a 6×3-foot poster divided into 12 numbered squares. In the first hour each person draws one concrete step of the target skill (e.g., tying a knot) inside their square using only colored pencils and tape. They then walk the wall in a silent "gallery walk," noting questions or gaps on sticky notes. In the second hour the group revisits the wall, pairs of learners swap squares, and they annotate one another’s step with corrections or clarifications. After 30 minutes they tape a final horizontal arrow across the wall showing the agreed correct order. Success is observable when the completed wall is a coherent, numbered sequence with zero unresolved sticky notes and every participant can recite the full sequence aloud without the wall in under two minutes.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Each participant brings a real-life item (e.g., a bill, recipe) needing the skill. In session 1, pairs swap items and draft a 10-step 'how-to' guide using only pens and paper. Guides are posted on the wall. In session 2, each person performs the skill using a randomly assigned guide while the author silently observes and records one 'works' and one 'fix' on a shared tally sheet. At the end, the tally sheet shows total successful completions and visible improvement notes, making learning gains immediately countable.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Each participant receives an index card bearing one step of the skill, shuffled randomly. At the first meeting they form a human flowchart: holding hands in sequence order they physically walk through the steps, verbally explaining each. After each run-through they rotate cards and repeat. At the second meeting they create a single A3 poster showing the entire sequence with drawings and arrows; each person draws only their assigned step. Observers can see whether the poster is coherent and whether the group can silently re-enact the full sequence by pointing to each card in order.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Create a 90-minute “Story-Chain Walk” using the empty room and six volunteers. Two volunteers map a 1 km safe loop of streets; the other four prepare six numbered cards describing a local memory or skill. On day 14, pairs of residents receive one card, walk the loop together, and add their own brief anecdote to the card. Every 15 minutes the pairs swap cards at checkpoints, each time meeting a new stranger. Volunteers manage timing and collect the finished cards. Back in the room, cards are taped on a wall forming a shared community map. Total cost: 25 euros for paper, tape, markers, and water. The chain guarantees each participant exchanges stories with five new people, producing an enduring, visible record of connections.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Method: 'Skill Swap Carousel'. Session 1: Each of 12 learners brings one simple step of the target skill, written on a card. They form four trios; each trio teaches its step to the next, rotating every 12 minutes until every group has practiced all four steps. Session 2: Trios recombine into two hexagons; each hexagon merges the four steps into one complete sequence and rehearses it three times, then swaps sequences with the other hexagon for final practice. Observable success: every participant can demonstrate the full sequence to a partner in under five minutes without notes.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants label each item "repair," "re-purpose," or "donate." One volunteer shows a 5-minute quick-fix demo (tape, glue, clamp) on a single object; others copy at their own pace. A "confidence corner" offers pre-labeled parts bins and picture cards so novices work independently. After 30 minutes, a silent vote with colored dots marks finished pieces; any dot majority sends the object to donate, preventing false promises. Success is tallied by counting dots: ≥60 % repair/re-purpose equals success.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: The group builds a 'Tool-Swap Carousel': (1) Lay objects on the table; each participant draws a card naming one simple task (tighten, glue, clean, decorate) rather than 'fix the whole thing.' (2) After 10 minutes, objects rotate clockwise; the next person adds one new action or passes. (3) A red 'halt card' lets anyone stop work on an item that feels unsafe or futile, moving it to a clearly marked 'Parts Harvest' bin. (4) At the end, the group photographs working items and weighs the bin; success equals >50 % of objects either functioning again or fully harvested for parts, plus every participant naming at least one task they completed.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A "Shared Story Wall" where volunteers first collect six-word memories from residents via door-to-door postcards. On day 7, they pin every card anonymously on a donated corkboard in the empty room. Residents visit freely over the next week, reading stories and adding sticky-note replies or sketches next to any card that resonates. Each reply automatically creates a visible thread; when three replies accumulate, those neighbors are invited to a 45-minute "coffee-corner" chat in the same room using the 300 € for simple refreshments. Threads and photos stay on the wall, turning fleeting glances into an expanding, self-updating map of local connections.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants form a circle; each brings one personal example of a skill they already perform (e.g., tying a knot, folding a map). In round one, every person silently demonstrates their skill once while the others sketch the steps on a shared sheet of paper. In round two, each learner swaps sheets and attempts to replicate the skill from the drawings alone, marking any unclear step with a question mark. The group then collectively re-draws the ambiguous steps until all twelve sheets contain only unambiguous sequences. Success is observable: after 120 minutes every participant can perform at least one new skill without verbal prompts or reference to the original demonstrator, verified by a final silent round where each learner performs the newly acquired skill for the group.

problem: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Participants create a rotating peer-teaching cycle. In session 1, each learner receives one numbered index card naming a sequential sub-skill (e.g., “knot-tying step 3”). Using only paper, pencils and string, learners silently sketch or fold a one-minute demo of their step, then pair-teach clockwise for five minutes; receivers immediately practice and initial the card if understood. After two full rotations, cards are shuffled and re-dealt for verification. Session 2 repeats the cycle with tougher sub-skills. Success is visible: completed physical samples (knots, folds, circuits) that match a master key drawn on the wall, plus peer-initialed cards showing each learner has both taught and been signed off on every step.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Residents receive a numbered envelope with a single sentence prompt and a blank postcard. They write a short story or memory, then hand it to the next-numbered volunteer who adds a sentence and passes it on until six contributions form one collective postcard. The final postcard is photocopied and mailed back to each participant within the fortnight, creating a tangible keepsake that records shared creativity and establishes an ongoing pen-pal loop for future exchanges.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A rotating-story quilt: six volunteers cut 25×25 cm fabric squares from cheap bed sheets. Each participant receives one square and writes or draws a personal memory. Squares are passed daily among volunteers and any drop-in residents for two weeks, collecting 60–80 squares. Every evening they are pinned to a wall grid in the empty room, forming a growing visual map. On day 14 a communal sewing bee joins squares into a single quilt using borrowed needles and thread; the finished quilt is hung permanently as a town artifact. Total cost: 80 € for fabric, thread and safety pins; all other items are donated or lent.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Neighborhood repair circle: lay objects on table; each participant draws a token labeled “try,” “adapt,” or “harvest.” “Try” holders get 15 min with tools; “adapt” holders sketch one non-original use; “harvest” holders disassemble for parts. A “pause bell” rings if anyone feels stuck—object returns to table without stigma. After one round, tally three metrics on a shared sheet: objects still usable, parts salvaged, participants who engaged. Target: at least 60 % combined score. Unfinished items go to a labeled “parts library” box for future circles, ensuring nothing is discarded today.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: ‘Recipe Swap & Story Circle’ – six volunteers set up a low-cost kitchen table in the empty room. Each resident brings one household ingredient or utensil. In pairs they exchange recipes, prepare one shared dish, then sit together to eat and tell the story behind the meal. Tables rotate every 15 minutes so everyone meets four new people. Budget covers €50 for basic spices, €100 for reusable plates/cutlery, €150 for printed recipe cards and name tags. Activity runs one Saturday afternoon, 2–5 pm, within two weeks; cleanup is shared, creating immediate common ground and a printed cookbook of contacts for future meet-ups.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A "Repair or Retell" circle: participants lay objects on the table; each briefly states its story. The group then votes to repair (if a fix is obvious within 10 min using tools) or to repurpose (cutting, painting, or combining parts). A "red card" safeguard lets anyone pause work if safety or skill concerns arise. Success is measured by tallying repaired items plus repurposed pieces that leave with a new owner or shared artwork; a quick show-of-hands at close confirms perceived confidence gain.

problem: A small town has an empty room, a budget of 300 euros, and six volunteers. Design one original activity that helps residents who do not know each other build lasting connections. It must start within two weeks and require no specialist equipment. Describe the mechanism, participation and resources. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: A 120-minute "Story Jar Exchange" starts in the empty room. Each of the six volunteers brings one household object (cup, scarf, photo, etc.) and one written 100-word memory tied to it. Volunteers sit in a circle; each places their item in the communal jar. Participants draw an item at random, read its memory aloud, then improvise a one-minute continuation or twist. After three rounds, everyone swaps contact details and agrees on a shared WhatsApp group for future micro-meet-ups. Budget covers a 5-euro jar, 3 euros for slips of paper, and 2 euros for tea; leftover funds buy biscuits. No specialist tools needed; the mechanism relies solely on personal objects and storytelling to forge immediate, repeatable bonds.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Lay out a Repair-or-Recycle Fair: mark three zones—Fix, Learn, and Scrap—around the table. Each participant picks an object, uses a quick two-minute “can-I-fix?” checklist (needs only hand tools, <10 min, spare parts on table). If yes, they attempt repair in Fix; if no or they prefer, they move to Learn to disassemble for parts or art, or to Scrap to sort materials for local recycling pickup. A visible timer and color-coded cards limit turns, ensuring fair access. Success is tallied by (a) items diverted from landfill, (b) number of first-time fixers who finish unaided, logged on a shared whiteboard; both counts posted at end of day.

problem: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.
proposal: Place objects on the shared table as a silent exhibition. Each participant writes one anonymous note: either a repair idea, an artistic repurposing, or a 'no fix' label. Notes are read aloud; the group votes only on objects with at least two repair or repurposing suggestions. Chosen items receive a 30-minute time-boxed group effort using available tools; the rest stay untouched. A visible tally board records 'fixed', 'repurposed', and 'set aside' counts. Success is measured by whether ≥70 % of participants add at least one note and whether ≥50 % of objects receive a documented new fate, proving engagement without over-promising repairs.
